narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated an 82% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain; it means the model found the risk high enough that admission was not supported under the school’s process.

The strongest factor was your third-year decile: at 1.00, you were at the very bottom of your class, far below the accepted-student average of about 5.79. This pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your first-year decile was the second strongest factor and also pointed toward failure: at 1.00, you were again far below the accepted average of about 6.00. The third factor, your undergraduate GPA of 3.20, worked in the opposite direction: it was only slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, and slightly reduced the predicted risk, but not enough to offset the two class-decile signals.

To improve a future application, focus on what can be strengthened and explained. Provide updated evidence of academic readiness, such as strong upper-level grades or a clear upward trend if available, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can prepare to raise it meaningfully. Seek advising about bar-exam preparation and whether a conditional-admission path or post-baccalaureate coursework could demonstrate reduced risk. You may also ask whether the decision can be reviewed with additional context, but the clearest path is to build newer evidence that addresses the academic concerns the model weighted most heavily.
